question: What are the latest developments in the past 30 days on U.S. export controls affecting NVIDIA's data center GPU sales to China, and what does NVIDIA's own Q3 FY2027 outlook assume about China?
grading: Reference-free. Key points: (1) every development dated and within window; (2) quotes/paraphrases NVIDIA's own stated China assumption from the Q2 FY27 outlook; (3) clearly separates company statements from media/analyst speculation; (4) no uncited causal claims about revenue impact
answer: Snapshot: September 2–October 1, 2026. September 9: C4ADS published evidence of restricted NVIDIA chips reaching China through institutional purchases and Southeast Asian trade networks; this is an enforcement-gap report, not a new U.S. rule. [G13-E1] September 28: Ars, citing The Information, reported China considering RTX Pro 5500 purchases by Alibaba and ByteDance; approval was uncertain and this concerns Chinese import policy, not a confirmed U.S. export-rule change. [G13-E2] The reviewed sources do not establish a newly enacted U.S. control in this window. Separately, NVIDIA’s August 26 outlook assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China in Q3 FY2027, within its USD 108 billion ±2% total-revenue guide. That company statement is older context and remains distinct from September reporting. [G13-E3]

output.answer:
Here are the latest developments on U.S. export controls affecting NVIDIA’s data-center GPU sales to China, and what the company’s own guidance assumes.

## Recent Export-Control Developments (past ~30 days)

**No policy easing from the U.S.-China summit.**  
The White House summit on September 24, 2026, did not result in any relaxation of semiconductor export controls. National-security export controls were reportedly taken off the trade-talk table, and Beijing’s summit deliverables did not mention them [[1]](https://financefeeds.com/nvidia-nvda-price-prediction-227-169-383).

**H200 remains a capped, licensed exception; Blackwell stays banned.**  
NVIDIA’s older-generation H200 (and AMD’s MI325X) are still eligible for case-by-case U.S. export licensing to China under a January 2026 Commerce Department rule, subject to performance ceilings, third-party testing, and volume caps. However, NVIDIA’s newer Blackwell data-center chips (B100, B200, GB200) remain under a presumption of denial and are effectively banned from China [[2]](https://tech-insider.org/china-modded-rtx-5090-96gb-vram-alibaba-2026)[[3]](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/billions-worth-of-export-restricted-ai-accelerators-sold-to-china-report-details-how-chinese-firms-skirt-trumps-regulations).

**Beijing is blocking purchases even when Washington allows them.**  
Although the U.S. approved H200 sales to roughly 10 Chinese companies (including Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, and JD.com) in May—with a 25% tariff and volume limits—Chinese authorities have reportedly guided domestic firms to refrain from buying in order to nurture homegrown suppliers like Huawei. Consequently, H200 shipments to China represented less than 1% of NVIDIA’s Data Center revenue in Q2 FY2027, and no meaningful deliveries have materialized [[4]](https://finance.biggo.com/news/c40c9fc3-90fb-4176-bd15-db35b8a64b8f)[[5]](https://www.barchart.com/story/news/4863560/bytedance-could-buy-1-million-nvidia-gpus-but-don-t-bank-on-it-yet).

**Gray-market enforcement gaps persist.**  
Investigative reports in September detailed how billions of dollars in export-restricted NVIDIA accelerators are still reaching Chinese end users through subsidiary networks in Southeast Asia (e.g., Malaysia-based Speedmatrix and Inspur-linked Aivres) and schemes involving Hong Kong trading firms and Chinese universities with defense/intelligence ties [[6]](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/billions-worth-of-export-restricted-ai-accelerators-sold-to-china-report-details-how-chinese-firms-skirt-trumps-regulations)[[7]](https://tech-insider.org/megaspeed-speedmatrix-malaysia-nvidia-chips-2026).

**NVIDIA is testing non-data-center pathways.**  
China is reportedly considering allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to purchase NVIDIA’s **RTX Pro 5500**, a professional workstation GPU aimed at AI workloads on PCs rather than server farms. Because this is not classified as a data-center chip, it may fall outside current restrictions, though the U.S. government has not publicly ruled on it [[8]](https://simplywall.st/stocks/us/semiconductors/nasdaq-nvda/nvidia/future)[[9]](https://www.barchart.com/story/news/4863560/bytedance-could-buy-1-million-nvidia-gpus-but-don-t-bank-on-it-yet).

## What NVIDIA’s Q3 FY2027 Outlook Assumes About China

**Zero China Data Center revenue is baked into guidance.**  
When NVIDIA issued its Q3 FY2027 outlook in late August 2026, it explicitly stated: **“NVIDIA is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in its outlook.”** This assumption has not been revised in any subsequent release through late September [[10]](https://simplywall.st/stocks/us/semiconductors/nasdaq-nvda/nvidia/future)[[11]](https://news.alphastreet.com/nvidia-nvda-ai-leadership-faces-a-yield-and-valuation-reality-check)[[12]](https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/09/10/got-10000-eli-lilly-vs-nvidia-the-better-buy-for-2026).

**The numbers.**  
The company guided Q3 FY2027 revenue to approximately **$108 billion (±2%)**, with gross margin around 74.0%. None of that forecast includes Chinese data-center sales. NVIDIA management continues to treat any potential China recovery as upside optionality, not a base-case driver [[13]](https://finance.biggo.com/news/c40c9fc3-90fb-4176-bd15-db35b8a64b8f)[[14]](https://seekingalpha.com/article/4949973-china-wont-move-chip-stocks-anymore).

In short, although Washington and Beijing have both shown minor flexibility around the edges, NVIDIA’s near-term financial plan treats the Chinese data-center market as essentially closed.
